pages.title: Continental C85-12 at a glance
pages.summary: The numbers you'll reach for most. Keep this page dog-eared.
steps: Four cylinders, two plugs each: eight plugs, two magnetos.
Cylinders count 1 to 4 from the front: odd numbers on the right, even on the left.
Firing order is 1-3-2-4.
Turn the prop by hand only in the direction of rotation, and only with both mags OFF and the P-leads good.

specs.Oil: 4-1/2 qt; SAE 40 above 40 F, SAE 20 below
specs.Mag drop: 125 rpm max, 50 rpm max between mags

pages.title: Safetying
pages.summary: Anything that can back out gets safety wire, a cotter pin, or a self-locking nut.
steps: Wire pulls in the tightening direction: if the nut tried to loosen, the wire would have to stretch.
Twist 6 to 8 turns per inch, pigtail 3 to 6 twists, bend it back so it won't snag.
Never reuse safety wire or a cotter pin.
Elastic stop nuts: replace them when you can spin them on by hand.

pages.title: Oil change and suction screen
pages.summary: Every 25 hours on a C-85 with no oil filter. The screen tells you how the engine's wearing.
steps: Run the engine to warm the oil so it drains clean.
Pan under the sump. Cut the safety wire and pull the drain plug.
While it drains, pull the suction screen and set it aside for inspection (see Oil screen).
New gasket on the screen and the drain plug. Torque, then safety-wire both.
Fill four and a half quarts at the filler. Run it, check for leaks, recheck the dipstick.

pages.title: Chafed wire
pages.summary: A wire rubbing on a bracket wears through and shorts.
steps: Battery off.
Cut out the damaged section. Strip, crimp a butt splice each end, heat-shrink over it.
Add a cushioned clamp so it can't reach the edge again.

pages.title: Battery
pages.summary: Won't crank, everything's dead.
steps: Master off. Negative terminal first.
New battery, positive terminal first.
Check the generator charges on the run-up.

pages.title: Starter
pages.summary: Just clicks: the starter or its drive is seized.
steps: Battery off. Leads off the starter.
Starter out, new one in, leads on. Test it.

pages.title: Radio and antenna
pages.summary: Dead radio: start with the antenna and coax.
steps: Check the coax connector at both ends.
Replace a broken antenna. Radio check on the ground.

pages.title: Aileron and elevator cable tension
pages.summary: Slack cables give sloppy controls; tight ones wear the pulleys.
steps: Inspection plate off. Clamp the tensiometer on the cable away from the turnbuckle.
Cut the safety wire. Turn the barrel to bring the tension into range.
No more than three threads showing outside the barrel at either end.
New safety wire, then check full travel both ways.

pages.title: Trim cable
pages.summary: The trim cable rides a drum with a jackscrew. It runs dry.
steps: Never oil a trim cable: oil holds grit and the cable slips on the drum.
Clean it with a dry rag. Replace it if it's frayed or gummed.
Set the tension and check the trim moves stop to stop.
pages.caution: Oil on a trim cable fails the job.

pages.title: Rudder cables
pages.summary: Stiff rudder pedals: a frayed or jammed cable at a pulley.
steps: Run a rag along the cable: frayed wires catch the cloth.
Replace the cable, set tension, safety the turnbuckles.

pages.title: Gascolator (fuel strainer)
pages.summary: The bowl catches water and grit before they reach the carburetor.
steps: Fuel OFF.
Cut the safety wire. Back off the thumb nut and swing the bail down.
Bowl and screen out. Wash both in clean fuel.
New cork gasket. Bowl up, bail over, thumb nut snug by hand.
Safety-wire the nut to the bail. Fuel ON, check for drips.

pages.title: Water in the fuel
pages.summary: Water is heavier than gas: it sits in the bottom of the bowl and the tank.
steps: Sump the gascolator drain into a clear tester before every flight.
Water shows as clear beads or a layer under the blue fuel.
Keep draining until the cup comes out all blue. If it never clears, drain the tank.

pages.title: Fuel cap vent
pages.summary: The tank needs air in as fuel goes out. A plugged vent starves the engine in flight.
steps: The vent tube on the cap points forward into the wind.
Mud daubers love it. Pull the nest, run a wire through, blow it clear.
Check it on every walk-around.

pages.title: Stale fuel
pages.summary: Gas left for years turns to varnish and smells like old paint.
steps: Drain the tank completely through the gascolator.
Pull the bowl and screen and clean them (see Gascolator).
Fill with fresh avgas, sump again, and look for varnish flakes.

pages.title: Fuel line
pages.summary: Tank to gascolator to carburetor, gravity fed. No pump on a Cub.
steps: Fuel OFF. Drain the line into a can.
Break the B-nuts at each end with two wrenches: one holds the fitting.
Route the new line clear of the exhaust. Clamp it so it can't chafe.
Fuel ON, look for stains at every fitting.

pages.title: Landing gear bungee cords
pages.summary: Rubber shock cords are the Cub's only suspension. They age whether it flies or not.
steps: Read the two colored threads in the cover: year and quarter of manufacture.
Over five years old, a cracked cover, or the plane sits low: replace both sides.
Jack the fuselage so the gear hangs. Stretch the old rings off with the bungee tool.
Stretch new rings over both spools. Jack down and check the stance.
pages.caution: A bungee under tension can take a finger off. Never put your hand between the spools.

pages.title: Tailwheel
pages.summary: The tailwheel steers with the rudder through two springs and short chains.
steps: Check the leaf spring for cracks, mostly in the top leaf near the mount.
Steering springs should hold their coils closed with a little slack in the chain.
Wipe the old grease off the fitting, then grease it until fresh grease shows.

pages.title: Bleeding the brakes
pages.summary: Expander-tube brakes: fluid swells a rubber tube that pushes the blocks against the drum.
steps: Cap off the bleeder at the top of the wheel. Clear hose from the bleeder into a jar of fluid.
Open the bleeder a half turn. Pump the pedal slowly.
Keep going until the fluid in the hose runs with no bubbles.
Close the bleeder, cap on. Top up the reservoir with red fluid.

pages.title: Main tires
pages.summary: Low-pressure 8.00-4 tires: the Cub's big soft tires are what let it land on grass.
steps: Jack the axle. Deflate fully before you split the wheel.
New tube, a little talc, line the valve up with the slot.
Inflate to seat the bead, deflate, then inflate to pressure.

pages.title: Door hinge pin
pages.summary: Rusted solid pins take patience.
steps: Soak with penetrant, wait, soak again.
Drive it out. New pin, new cotter.

pages.title: Windshield
pages.summary: Cracked windshields spread.
steps: Retainer screws out, old windshield out.
Fit the new one, drill oversize holes so it can expand, screws snug only.

pages.title: Wing rigging
pages.summary: The front strut fork sets dihedral; the rear sets wash-out.
steps: Dihedral: stretch a string tip to tip across the top of the wings. Measure the gap at the root; both sides should match.
Wash-out: a block and a level on the tip rib, then the root rib. The tip should sit at a lower angle than the root.
Out of spec: loosen the jam nut, turn the fork in or out a turn at a time, then lock the jam nut.

pages.title: Tail brace wires
pages.summary: Wires brace the fin and stabilizer against each other.
steps: Check for rust, bends, and bowing in flight-loaded positions.
Replace in pairs. Tighten until the wires are taut with no flutter, both sides equal.

pages.title: Dressing a nick (metal props)
pages.summary: A stone nick is a crack waiting to start. Dress it out smooth.
steps: File across the edge, never into it. Blend the nick into a smooth, shallow scallop about ten times as long as it is deep.
Finish with emery cloth so no file marks are left.
Too deep, or near the tip or the hub? Retire the prop.

pages.title: Propeller tracking
pages.summary: Both tips should follow the same path. Out of track shakes the engine.
steps: Mags OFF. Set a block just under the tip of one blade, pencil a mark where it passes.
Rotate the prop, bring the other blade down, mark again.
More than 1/16 in apart: check the mounting bolts and the hub face.

pages.title: Propeller change
pages.summary: Bent blade: replace it. Don't straighten.
steps: Mags OFF. Cut the safety wire, remove the prop bolts.
New prop on the hub, bolts in, torque in a cross pattern.
Safety-wire the bolts. Track it.

pages.title: Compression test
pages.summary: Differential test: put 80 psi in, read what the cylinder holds.
steps: Engine warm. Top plug out. Turn the cylinder to top dead center on compression.
Hook up the tester and hold the prop. It will try to turn.
Read the gauge. Around 60/80 or below, or well under the others: listen for the leak.
Air at the exhaust: exhaust valve. Air at the air filter: intake valve. Air at the oil filler: rings.
pages.caution: Hold the prop firmly. At top center with air in, it can kick.

pages.title: Finding a cold cylinder
pages.summary: A cylinder that isn't firing stays cold.
steps: Mark each exhaust stack with a temperature crayon.
Short run at idle and a bit above.
The mark that didn't melt is your dead cylinder: check its plugs, leads, and intake connector.

pages.title: Bringing an engine out of storage
pages.summary: Dehydrator plugs, desiccant bags and preservative oil kept it from rusting.
steps: Read the tag. Count every plug and bag on it, so none are left in.
Pull the bags from the intake and exhaust.
Pull the dehydrator plugs. Pink crystals mean it got damp: look in with a light for rust.
Wipe off the preservative, change the oil, then pre-oil before the first start.
pages.caution: A desiccant bag left in the intake will be sucked into the engine.

pages.title: Pre-oiling a dry engine
pages.summary: An engine that sat for years has no oil on the cam. Cranking it dry wipes the lifters.
steps: Pull a plug from each cylinder so it turns easily.
Pressure pot on the oil gallery. Pump until oil shows at the rocker boxes.
Turn the prop by hand a few blades. Plugs back in, then start it.

pages.title: Air filter and carb heat box
pages.summary: Dirty filters rob power. A worn heat valve lets unfiltered air in.
steps: Four screws, cover off. Filter out.
Hold it to the light: if you can't see through it, replace it.
Work the carb heat valve. It should close tight both ways.
New filter, cover on.

pages.title: Spark test
pages.summary: Find the dead lead: no spark means no fire.
steps: Top plugs out, leads left on. Lay each plug on the crankcase so its shell is grounded.
Turn the prop through. Each plug should snap a blue spark.
No spark: try another plug on that lead. Still no spark, the lead is bad.
pages.caution: Mags HOT for this test. Keep everyone clear of the prop.

pages.title: Reading spark plugs
pages.summary: Keep the plugs in order: each one tells you about its cylinder.
steps: Tan or light gray: healthy.
Dry black soot: running rich, or a weak spark on that plug.
Wet and oily: oil past the rings or the valve guides.
Thin, worn electrodes: worn out. Replace the set.
Rotate top and bottom plugs at each cleaning so they wear evenly.

pages.title: Changing spark plugs
pages.summary: Runs rough and puffs black smoke: fouled plugs.
steps: Plugs out, in order. New copper gaskets.
Gap check, a dab of anti-seize on the threads, not on the first thread.
Torque, leads back on, run-up.

pages.title: Hot magneto
pages.summary: A broken P-lead means the mag stays live with the switch OFF. The prop can fire.
steps: Mag check with no drop on one mag: treat it as hot.
Hang a DANGER tag on the prop right away.
Find the broken P-lead and replace it. Check the mag shuts off on the run-up.
pages.caution: Never turn the prop of an engine with a hot mag.

pages.title: Timing the magnetos
pages.summary: Each mag must fire exactly 28 degrees before top center.
steps: Cowl off. Clip the timing light to the mag's P-lead terminal and to ground.
Bring No. 1 up on compression. Back up, then come forward slowly to 28 deg BTC on the marks.
The light should come on right as you reach the mark. Early or late: loosen the mag hold-down nuts and rotate the mag.
Tighten, check again, both mags.

pages.title: Magneto change
pages.summary: Dies on the mag check: the mag is bad.
steps: Mags OFF. P-lead and harness off, two hold-down nuts off, mag out.
New gasket. Install the new mag and time it (see Timing).

pages.title: Cooling baffles
pages.summary: The baffles force air down through the fins. Every gap is a hot cylinder.
steps: Clean packed dirt, straw, and bugs from between the fins.
Replace torn seal strips. They must lie against the cowl, curled toward the high-pressure side.

pages.title: Bird nest
pages.summary: Nests in the cowl block cooling air and burn on hot cylinders.
steps: Cowl off. Pull every bit of nest out, including what's fallen between the fins.
Check the intake and the baffles before you button it up.

pages.title: Exhaust and heat muff
pages.summary: A cracked muffler leaks carbon monoxide into the cabin heat.
steps: Scat hose and heat muff off.
Look for cracks and gray-white stains fanning from them.
Cracked: replace the muffler. Don't weld it.
Shroud and hose back on.
pages.caution: Carbon monoxide has no smell. A crack you missed can kill the pilot.

pages.title: Reading the oil screen
pages.summary: What's caught in the screen is the engine telling you what's wearing.
steps: Rinse the screen in solvent over a clean white towel.
Run a magnet through what's on the towel.
Steel (sticks to the magnet): cam, lifters, crank, cylinder walls. A few flakes, watch it. A pile, ground it.
Aluminum (won't stick, bright): pistons or the case. Bronze (won't stick, gold): bushings.
Log what you found. Same amount next oil change is fine; more is a teardown.

pages.title: Oil leaks
pages.summary: Oil on the belly is normal on a C-85; oil on the windshield is not.
steps: Wipe the engine clean, run it, then look for the fresh wet line.
Rocker covers: new cork gasket, snug the screws evenly. Don't crush the cork.
Pushrod tube seals and the sump gasket are next most likely. Oil on the prop and windshield: front crank seal.
